summary: Specifies the RSVP diagnostic facility, which lets a user collect information about RSVP state along a path through the network. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: It is like asking every stop on a bus route what reservations they have, so you can see where a problem is.

questions: what is an rsvp diagnostic message
what is dreq and drep in rsvp
what is a last-hop node in rsvp
subtitle: A query-and-reply facility that collects RSVP state hop by hop along a path, for debugging and resource management.

tldr.problem: In basic RSVP, error messages are the only feedback a host gets, and they carry only information from the failed point, with nothing about state at other hops or about how reservations are merged.
tldr.mechanism: A Diagnostic Request (DREQ) travels hop by hop from a LAST-HOP node toward the sender, each RSVP-capable hop adds a DIAG_RESPONSE object, and the result returns to the requester in Diagnostic Reply (DREP) messages.
tldr.outcome: Users can see flowspecs, refresh timers, merges and non-RSVP clouds along a path without changing any RSVP state; it is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 2745 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the base RSVP specification in RFC 2205.

sections.title: Why RSVP Needs Diagnostics
sections.content:
In the basic RSVP protocol, error messages are the only way an end host learns about a failure when setting up path state or reservation state. An error carries only information from the failed point. Even without failures, a host gets no details about a reservation that has been put in place, such as whether, where or how its request is merged with others.

The RSVP diagnostic facility fills that gap. It collects and reports RSVP state along the path from a receiver to a specific sender, using messages that are independent of other RSVP control messages and have no side effects: they change no state at nodes or hosts, and they report information rather than errors.

The goals are to collect state from every RSVP-capable hop (flowspecs, refresh timer values and reservation merging), to collect the IP hop count across each non-RSVP cloud, and to avoid diagnostic packet implosion or explosion. Checking resource availability along a path is an explicit non-goal.
sections.eli5: Normally you only hear "something went wrong" from the place that broke. This lets you ask every stop along the way what it knows.

sections.title: How a Diagnostic Query Travels
sections.content:
Two new RSVP message types are introduced: Diagnostic Request (DREQ) and Diagnostic Reply (DREP). A client on a requester host, which need not take part in the session, sends a DREQ toward the LAST-HOP node, which should be on the RSVP path being diagnosed. From there the DREQ moves hop by hop toward the sender, and each RSVP-capable hop adds a DIAG_RESPONSE object with its local RSVP state for the session.

When it reaches the ending node, normally the sender, the message type becomes DREP and the result goes to the requester. A client can limit the path segment with a hop-count limit. Partial responses can be returned early if an error such as "no path state" stops forwarding. All diagnostic packets are forwarded by unicast only, to avoid implosion or explosion.

A DREP can return directly or hop by hop along the reverse path, using the optional ROUTE object. The direct return is faster and more efficient, but hop-by-hop may be the only choice if packets must cross firewalls. A DREQ is always a single unfragmented IP datagram, but one DREQ can produce several DREP packets, each a fragment of the whole reply. DREQ packets can only be forwarded once RSVP path state exists; without it, the text suggests traceroute or mtrace.
sections.eli5: You hand a clipboard to the last stop on a route. It passes it back toward the start, each stop adds a line, and the finished list is mailed back to you.

sections.title: Diagnostic Message Layout
sections.content:
DREQ and DREP messages consist of the RSVP Common Header followed by objects in a fixed order: the Session object, a Next-Hop RSVP_HOP object, a DIAGNOSTIC object, an optional DIAG_SELECT object, an optional ROUTE object, and zero or more DIAG_RESPONSE objects. The Common Header uses Type 8 for DREQ and Type 9 for DREP. In a DREP fragment with the MF flag set, the RSVP length field gives the length of that single fragment, not of the complete reply.

The Next-Hop RSVP_HOP object carries the logical interface handle through which the DREQ should be received at the upstream node, and is updated at each hop. It serves the same purpose as the RSVP_HOP in a RESV message: telling logical interfaces apart and avoiding problems from routing asymmetries and non-RSVP clouds.
sections.eli5: Every diagnostic message has the same set of boxes in the same order, so each stop knows exactly where to look and where to add its own note.

sections.title: The Control and Response Objects
sections.content:
The DIAGNOSTIC object (Class 30, C-Type 1 for IPv4 and 2 for IPv6) holds shared control data. Max-RSVP-hops limits how far to collect (zero means no limit; 1 means start and end nodes are the same), and RSVP-hop-count records hops so far. The MF flag means "more fragments" and is zero in every DREQ. Request ID ties a request to its reply fragments, Path MTU is a default size for diagnostic messages, and Fragment Offset says where a DREP fragment belongs. The object also carries the LAST-HOP address, a SENDER_TEMPLATE for the sender being traced and a Requester FILTER_SPEC with the address and port for replies.

The optional DIAG_SELECT object (Class 33) lists [Class, C-Type] pairs naming which RSVP objects each node should report; a C-Type of zero is a wildcard. Without it, a default set is reported: SENDER_TSPEC, FILTER_SPEC, FLOWSPEC and STYLE. The optional ROUTE object (Class 31) records the DREQ's path and is used in reverse as a source route; if absent, replies go directly to the requester.

Each node adds a DIAG_RESPONSE object (Class 32). It holds the DREQ arrival time as a 32-bit NTP timestamp, incoming, outgoing and previous-hop addresses, D-TTL (the IP hops since the previous RSVP node), an M flag showing whether the reservation is merged with others, a 3-bit R-error code, the refresh timer multiple K, and the local refresh timer value in seconds. An optional TUNNEL object links an end-to-end session to the tunnel session at a tunnel exit.
sections.eli5: One box says how far to go and where to send the answer. Another says which facts to write down. Each stop fills in its own box with times, addresses and reservation details.

sections.title: Forwarding Rules and Fragmentation
sections.content:
A node that gets a DREQ builds a DIAG_RESPONSE: it works out the D-TTL by comparing the IP TTL with Send_TTL in the RSVP header, sets the arrival time and interface addresses, and raises the hop count. If there is no PATH state for the session, it sets R-error to "No PATH state" and stops. Otherwise it fills in the requested objects and, if hops remain and the node is not the sender, lowers Path MTU to the incoming interface MTU and forwards the DREQ toward the sender, appending its incoming interface to the ROUTE object if present. At the end of the path it turns the DREQ into a DREP.

To avoid relying on IP fragmentation, the requester sets a default Path MTU in the DREQ and nodes reduce it where needed. If adding another response would make the message too big, the node copies it into a DREP carrying the accumulated responses, sends it back with MF set, trims those responses from the DREQ, and carries on. If the ROUTE object itself becomes too big, it is replaced with an empty one and the "ROUTE object too big" error bit is set; later replies then go straight to the requester.

A DREP with a ROUTE object moves back by decrementing the R-pointer at each hop. If a DREP cannot be forwarded further it is simply dropped. IP fragmentation can still happen, for example when non-RSVP hops have smaller MTUs or a direct reply takes a different route.
sections.eli5: If the note gets too long for the envelope, a stop mails off what has been collected so far and starts a fresh page, so the envelope never has to be torn.

sections.title: Using the Facility to Find Problems
sections.content:
The RFC lists practical uses. Timer values at each hop help tell whether reservation state that keeps going up and down is caused by badly set timers, K values across lossy links, or routing changes. A D-TTL above one between adjacent RSVP nodes reveals a non-RSVP cloud, and the arrival timestamps give a rough, not necessarily accurate, idea of its size. If the flowspec in a downstream response is smaller than the one upstream, a reservation merge happened at that node. A receiver can also send a DREQ before reserving to learn how many RSVP hops there are and how many already hold reservations from others.

Complications are acknowledged. Across firewalls, a querier on a receiving host may first omit the ROUTE object for a faster reply and retry with one. For a third-party requester separated from the LAST-HOP by a firewall, the only suggestion is to pick a LAST-HOP on the requester's side. "Legacy" RSVP routers that do not understand diagnostics drop the messages, so the client gets no response; the suggested workaround is to use traceroute or mtrace and increase Max-RSVP-hops gradually. The RFC admits it has no complete solution for routing asymmetries that make this fail.
sections.eli5: If a bus is late, you can check each stop to see where the delay starts, whether a stop was skipped, or whether two groups booked the same seats.

sections.title: Building a Diagnostic Client
sections.content:
Network nodes should hold no more state than necessary, so they only forward diagnostic messages and fill in DIAG_RESPONSE objects. Everything else is the job of the diagnostic client, which does not need to run an RSVP daemon if it is a third-party host.

The client takes the session, last-hop, sender, Max-RSVP-hops and optional DIAG_SELECT list from the user, and sends a DREQ to the LAST-HOP as a raw IP message with protocol number 46. It includes an empty ROUTE object for hop-by-hop replies and puts its UDP listening port in the Requester FILTER_SPEC. It sets a retransmission timer, reassembles DREP fragments with a reassembly timer like IP's, retransmits a few times when nothing arrives, then falls back to traceroute or mtrace with increasing hop counts, and finally must notify the invoking entity if everything fails.
sections.eli5: The program asking the question does the waiting, the re-asking and the piecing-together, so the stops along the way stay simple.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: As with any diagnostic tool, RSVP diagnostics can reveal possibly sensitive RSVP state to unwanted third parties. The authors consider the threat minimal, since diagnostic messages have no side effects and cannot change RSVP state in nodes. They say this makes it a smaller threat than tools such as SNMP. Processing of diagnostic messages can also be disabled if it is felt to be a security risk.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can ask may learn who has booked what, but they cannot change the bookings, and a stop can simply refuse to answer.

items.label: No error
items.desc: Nothing went wrong at this node.

items.desc: The node has no path state for the session, so the DREQ cannot go further.

items.label: Packet too big
items.desc: Adding the response would exceed Path MTU, so a DREP fragment is returned.

items.label: ROUTE object too big
items.desc: The ROUTE object is trimmed so the DREQ can keep going.
